title: Enter Technikwelt Solothurn
text:
The museum displays about 10,000 exhibits from the history of radio, television and computers from the early years to the present.[1]

> "What we're seeing here are basically all predecessors to the apps we have on our smartphones today." — Violetta Vitacca, Museum Director: Transhelvetica[2]

Many of the exhibits were developed and produced in the Solothurn region, e.g. by Autophon or Anton Gunzinger.[1,3] The collection has a focus on history of technology made in Switzerland with products of Studer-Revox Paillard, Bolex, Crypto AG, Gretag. It also shows the main stages of computer history with examples of IBM mainframes, Cray supercomputers, Commodore home computers, personal computers from Apple and IBM. It claims to feature "one of the few complete Apple-collections worldwide".[4]

Part of the museum is a collection of 300 mechanical calculators of the Swiss collector Peter Regenass. Furthermore, it holds a large collection on the history of radio and television including a vast number of radio and TV sets, recording devices for audio and video and projectors including the Eidophor projectors used 1958 - 1999.Over time the Enter Museum has integrated other collections such as the Audiorama Montreux, which closed its doors in 2010[5] or the computer collection of the Swiss collector Robert Weiss[6] or Peter Beck. Its collection has been named as outstanding by the media, the Neue Zürcher Zeitung writes "It's hard to name a Computer that had any technical or commercial significance in the last 50 Years, which could not be viewed here".[7]

### Selected exhibits

Switzerland's first radio station that started regular emission in Lausanne as early as 26 February 1923.[8]

Early home computers such as Mark-8 minicomputer, Commodore PET 2001 or Apple 1

Mechanical calculators such as The Millionaire calculator and Curta.

Cryptographic devices of Crypto AG, Gretag and others including the Swiss Nema and the Russian Fialka

The Smaky-computer of Swiss engineer Jean-Daniel Nicoud and the Lilith Computer by Niklaus Wirth

The video projector Eidophor used 1958 – 1999.

The outdoor projector Spitlight used at the 1956 Olympic winter games in Cortina di Ampezzo.
